summary: For ages 8-9: read and write Roman numerals to 100 (I, V, X, L, C and their combinations, including subtractive pairs like IV, IX, XL, XC) and convert both ways to Hindu-Arabic numbers. The deeper aim is to appreciate BY CONTRAST that our base-ten system carries value by position and uses zero as a placeholder, which Roman numerals lack — making vivid why place value is powerful. Teach symbol values, then the additive rule (XVII = 10+5+1+1), then the subtractive rule (IV = 5-1) as the tricky exception, and run the contrast explicitly by trying to write numbers that need many repeated symbols, a very large number, and zero in Roman.
misconceptions: Pure additive thinking, writing 4 as IIII or 9 as VIIII instead of IV/IX.
Inventing invalid subtractive forms (IL for 49 instead of XLIX).
Misordering symbols or ignoring the subtractive-position rule.
Thinking Roman numerals have a zero or place value.
Reading a subtractive pair additively (IX as 11).

activities.title: Build-a-numeral bench with a contrast challenge
steps: Place or drag symbol tiles (I, V, X, L, C) into a row and read the value aloud as you build, e.g. XVII = 10+5+1+1 = 17.
When you write 4 as IIII or 9 as VIIII, notice it is flagged and rewrite it the valid subtractive way (IV = 5-1, IX = 10-1).
Convert both directions: given 44, build XLIV; given XLIV, read it as 40 + 4.

Take the contrast challenge: write 88 (LXXXVIII) and notice how many repeated symbols it needs; then try a very large number like 3,000 and see how unwieldy it becomes — within the taught symbols you would need a huge string of C's, and the usual Roman form MMM uses M, a symbol beyond those you are taught; then try to write zero and find there is NO symbol at all — each shown beside the compact base-ten numeral.
activities.insight: Roman numerals combine fixed symbol values by adding (and sometimes subtracting the smaller-before-larger pair); because they have no place value and no zero placeholder, numbers with many repeats become unwieldy, very large numbers become enormous strings or need symbols beyond the basic set, and zero cannot be written at all — which is exactly why position-carries-value and a placeholder zero are powerful inventions.

activities.title: Talk to a Roman accountant about why the system changed
steps: In role, interview a Roman merchant or scholar about how they wrote numbers and did sums.
Ask them to add two large numbers using only Roman numerals and notice where it gets hard.
Probe: why was there no way to write zero, and why did the world later adopt place value and zero?
Summarise in your own words what base-ten gives us that Roman numerals do not.
activities.insight: The history-of-number aim — that the numeral system changed over time to include zero and place value — can become meaningful through an unscripted 'why is this so hard?' exchange that carries the contrast the curriculum emphasises.

activities.title: Consolidate conversion with real artefacts and validity checks
steps: Read Roman numerals on real artefacts — clock faces, monument or building dates, book chapter numbers — and write their Hindu-Arabic values (note that many clocks show 4 as IIII, a traditional variant; the standard written form is IV).
Write given numbers (e.g. 44, 49, 88) in Roman numerals, choosing valid subtractive forms.
Decide which of several forms is valid for a number like 49 (XLIX, not IL) and explain why.
Explain aloud how the two 4s in 44 differ (40 and 4 by position) and why XLIV instead uses subtraction.
activities.insight: Fluent two-way conversion and recognising valid versus invalid forms consolidate the reading/writing skill, while explaining the two 4s in 44 reinforces the place-value contrast.

activities.title: Reference chart and annotated clock face
steps: Keep a symbol-to-value reference to hand (I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100).
Tap or point to each clock numeral to reveal its value and whether it is built additively or subtractively.
Use a side-by-side Roman | Hindu-Arabic chart to check your conversions, and a place-value chart alongside to see what Roman lacks.
activities.insight: A clear reference supports recall of symbol values and makes the additive/subtractive make-up of familiar numerals (like clock numbers) explicit.

checkQuestion: Ask: 'Read XLIV for me. Now tell me: how is the Roman way of writing forty-four different from the way we write 44? How do you know?'
checkAnswer: XLIV = 44 (XL = 40 by subtraction, IV = 4 by subtraction). It differs because Roman numerals combine symbols by value with no place value and no zero, whereas in 44 the two 4s mean different amounts (40 and 4) because of their POSITION, and we use 0 to hold empty places.
